docs.container.component: `Container` decides how a node's children are arranged.
It does not give a node children — a node can already hold them with no atoms composed on it
at all. An atom carrying only the link would carry nothing, so arrangement is the whole of it.
Where a node itself sits is a separate question, answered by `Transformable`.
```ts
import { node, add, Container, Transformable, placeChildren } from "game-kit"
const desk = node("desk", Container({ layout: "free" }))   // places nobody
add(desk, node("card", Transformable({ at: { x: 2, y: 0 } })))
placeChildren(desk).get("card")   // { x: 2, y: 0 } — the child's own pose stands
## Fields
- `layout` — the name of a registered RECORD of layout. The kit comes with two: `free` places
nobody and leaves each child its own `at`, `row` places everyone. Register your own through
`registerLayout` — just like a surface through `registerSurface`.
## Layout record
- `place(children)` — pose for each child, in order; `undefined` means "I don't place this",
then its own `at` stands. Only positions return — height, angle, or scale the record cannot
write by design: a point holds none of them.
- Gap and padding belong to the record, not the container. In a row a gap means something, in
a free layout — nothing, and a field most layouts cannot use gets misread.
- `padding` — air around the tight wrap of the content; only the second AREA reads it (see
`Spread`), and even a record that places nobody has it.
## Notes
- A layout that places overwrites the child's `at` rather than combining with it.
- Space is reserved for what will BE SEEN: a child with scale two takes two of its own widths
in a row, else it would overlap its neighbour.
- An unknown layout name places nobody rather than throwing, for the same reason an unknown
surface is skipped: a content mistake should not take the scene down with it.
docs.container.free: A record that refuses to place: each child from the list stands where its own pose put it.
This is the "put things anywhere" canvas, and it is not a mode or a second kind of
container — just the smallest possible layout record, returning emptiness for each child.
Children here — a real list, one line per node: id and pose land on the node exactly as
written. Compare it with `Row`: the tree is the same, down to the poses, only the layout's
docs.container.row: The same list and the same poses — and none of them survived: a layout that places, places.
Each child takes as much room as its own footprint needs, so a row is not a grid of equal
cells. A child with no box takes no width and is still placed — removing a box should not
docs.container.gap: A gap is a parameter of the RECORD, and here the record is registered in plain sight: a
`registerLayout` with a row of your own, while the container only names it. There is no `gap`
and do not search for it there: a field most layouts cannot use gets misread.
A gap stands BETWEEN neighbors — there are one fewer of them than children: a row of three
cards has two gaps, a row of one has none, and the edge cards get no air on the sides.
docs.container.spread: The other source of area. The desk has no box of its own — the surface lands on the tight
wrap of what it holds: drag a card away and the paint follows it; take the children away —
there is nothing left to paint on.
`padding` — air around that wrap, and it too is a field of the record: here it is carried by
the FREE record, the one that places nobody. Padding grows only the area — the children
docs.container.reserve: A promise the record keeps for each child: space is reserved for what will BE SEEN. The first
card carries a scale — grow it, and neighbors back away, because a row measures the scaled
The measure takes only the child's OWN scale: the owner's scale grows the whole row at once
and so does not change who sits where inside it.
